title: Safed
hook: a hill town in Galilee becomes the center of Jewish mysticism

segments.voice: Yesterday, Doña Gracia Nasi, who turned a trading network into a way out. Your line was la señora. Today, one of the places the road led.

A small town clings to a hilltop in the Galilee, in the north of the land of Israel. Stone houses, narrow lanes, a view down to the Sea of Galilee on a clear day. It is not a capital. It has no royal court. And yet, in the generations after the expulsion from Spain, scholars, poets and mystics walked up its slopes and stayed. Some had fled Spain or Portugal, some came from the Ottoman cities, some were born nearby. For a while this hill town was the place to learn the hidden side of the Torah.
screen: `A TOWN ON A GALILEE HILL.` → `NO CAPITAL, NO COURT.` → `SCHOLARS WALK UP AND STAY.`

segments.voice: Tzfat is the Hebrew name; in English it's often written Safed. Why there? Part of the answer is a mountain nearby, Meron, where tradition places the grave of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, the sage whom tradition names as the teacher behind the Zohar, a book at the heart of Kabbalah. To live near Meron was to live near the source, as the mystics saw it. Part of the answer is the land itself: for Jews who had lost Spain, living there meant commandments tied to the soil could be kept, and the ancient graves were close. And part of the answer is the people who gathered. In a short span, Tzfat drew a legal scholar who would write a code of Jewish law, a poet who would write a song still sung on Friday night, and a quiet teacher who would change how Jews think about creation and repair. We'll meet them over the next days. Running through that circle was a conviction that the exile was not only a disaster in the world, but a crack in something deeper, and that prayer, study and the commandments done with care could help heal it. Psalm 121 is headed a Song of Ascents, which tradition links to pilgrims going up to Jerusalem. Its first line fits a hill town too: "I will lift up mine eyes unto the mountains: from whence shall my help come?" Today Tzfat is still a town of synagogues, artists and students.
screen: `TZFAT, OR SAFED.` · `NEAR MERON AND ITS TRADITIONS.` · `A CIRCLE OF SCHOLARS GATHERS.` · then, large: `I WILL LIFT UP MINE EYES.`

segments.voice: See stone walls going from gray to gold as the light reaches them, a few voices singing low on the way to prayer, a lake below catching the first sun. Let your breath slow to the pace of that waking town, and if you pray, say the psalm's line: I will lift up mine eyes unto the mountains.
Tzfat. A hill town in the Galilee, near Meron, where scholars and mystics gathered after the expulsion from Spain. Today's word.
Your line: the mystic town. A hill with no court, and a circle that gathered anyway. Day nine hundred fifty-one, done.
